claim: Chloride ions bind to the extracellular ligand-binding domain of sweet/umami taste receptors (T1r).
source: Here, we describe Cl− ion binding and the response of taste receptor type 1 (T1r), a receptor family composing sweet/umami receptors.
evidence: The claim is supported by crystallographic data showing Cl− binding to T1r3 LBD, confirmed by anomalous scattering experiments with Br− substitution and wavelength-specific detection.

claim: The T1r2a/T1r3 heterodimer from medaka fish exhibited specific Cl− binding in the vicinity of the amino-acid-binding site in the ligand-binding domain (LBD) of T1r3.
source: The T1r2a/T1r3 heterodimer from the medaka fish, currently the sole T1r amenable to structural analyses, exhibited a specific Cl− binding in the vicinity of the amino-acid-binding site in the ligand-binding domain (LBD) of T1r3, which is likely conserved across species, including human T1r3.
evidence: Supported by crystallographic structure determination and anomalous scattering experiments showing Cl− binding site in T1r3 LBD.

claim: The Cl− binding site in T1r3 is likely conserved across species, including human T1r3.
source: The T1r2a/T1r3 heterodimer from the medaka fish, currently the sole T1r amenable to structural analyses, exhibited a specific Cl− binding in the vicinity of the amino-acid-binding site in the ligand-binding domain (LBD) of T1r3, which is likely conserved across species, including human T1r3.
evidence: Supported by sequence alignment showing conservation of key residues (Thr105 and surrounding motifs) across T1r3 from various species.

claim: Cl− binding induced a conformational change in T1r2a/T1r3LBD at sub- to low-mM concentrations.
source: The Cl− binding induced a conformational change in T1r2a/T1r3LBD at sub- to low-mM concentrations, similar to canonical taste substances.
evidence: Supported by FRET experiments showing increased FRET intensity upon Cl− addition with EC50 ~1 mM, and DSF showing thermal stabilization with apparent Kd ~110 µM.

claim: Oral Cl− application to mice increased impulse frequencies of taste nerves connected to T1r-expressing taste cells.
source: Furthermore, oral Cl− application to mice increased impulse frequencies of taste nerves connected to T1r-expressing taste cells and promoted their behavioral preferences attenuated by a T1r-specific blocker or T1r3 knock-out.
evidence: Supported by single fiber recordings from mouse chorda tympani nerve showing concentration-dependent responses to NMDG-Cl.

claim: Cl−-induced taste nerve responses were attenuated by a T1r-specific blocker (gurmarin).
source: Furthermore, oral Cl− application to mice increased impulse frequencies of taste nerves connected to T1r-expressing taste cells and promoted their behavioral preferences attenuated by a T1r-specific blocker or T1r3 knock-out.
evidence: Supported by nerve recording data showing significant reduction in Cl− responses after gurmarin treatment.

claim: Cl−-induced taste nerve responses were attenuated in T1r3 knock-out mice.
source: Furthermore, oral Cl− application to mice increased impulse frequencies of taste nerves connected to T1r-expressing taste cells and promoted their behavioral preferences attenuated by a T1r-specific blocker or T1r3 knock-out.
evidence: Supported by nerve recording data showing significantly lower responses to Cl− in T1r3-KO mice compared to wild-type mice.

claim: Cl− evokes taste sensations by binding to T1r, serving as another preferred salt taste pathway at low concentration.
source: These results suggest that the Cl− evokes taste sensations by binding to T1r, thereby serving as another preferred salt taste pathway at a low concentration.
evidence: Supported by integration of structural data showing Cl− binding, biophysical data showing conformational changes, nerve recording data showing T1r-mediated responses, and behavioral data showing preference.

claim: NaCl at low or high concentrations is preferably or aversively perceived through distinct pathways.
source: Salt taste sensation is multifaceted: NaCl at low or high concentrations is preferably or aversively perceived through distinct pathways.
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature on salt taste perception.

claim: Cl− is thought to participate in taste sensation through an unknown mechanism.
source: Cl− is thought to participate in taste sensation through an unknown mechanism.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge prior to the current study, supported by the lack of identified mechanisms in previous literature.

claim: The preferable taste of ~100 mM concentration of table salt is evoked by specific interaction between the epithelial sodium channel (ENaC) and sodium ion.
source: Regarding the salty taste, the preferable taste, ~100 mM concentration of table salt, is evoked by specific interaction between the epithelial sodium channel (ENaC) and sodium ion (Chandrashekar et al., 2010; Figure 1).
evidence: Supported by citation to Chandrashekar et al., 2010.

claim: Salt sensation exhibits multifaced properties, suggesting the existence of an adequate concentration range for salt intake to maintain the homeostasis of body fluid concentration.
source: Notably, salt sensation exhibits multifaced properties (Roper, 2015), thereby suggesting the existence of an adequate concentration range for salt intake to maintain the homeostasis of body fluid concentration.
evidence: Supported by citation to Roper, 2015 and inference about homeostasis.

claim: High concentrations of salt over levels perceived as a preferred taste, such as ~500 mM, stimulate bitter and sour taste cells and are perceived as an aversive taste.
source: For example, high concentrations of salt over levels perceived as a preferred taste, such as ~500 mM, stimulate bitter and sour taste cells and are perceived as an aversive taste (Oka et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Oka et al., 2013.

claim: Low salt concentrations under the 'preferable' concentration, such as several mM to a hundred mM concentrations, are perceived as sweet by human panels.
source: Conversely, low salt concentrations under the 'preferable' concentration, such as several mM to a hundred mM concentrations, are perceived as sweet by human panels (Bartoshuk et al., 1964; Bartoshuk et al., 1978; Cardello, 1979).
evidence: Supported by citations to Bartoshuk et al., 1964; Bartoshuk et al., 1978; Cardello, 1979.

claim: The mechanism of sweet perception at low salt concentrations has never been extensively pursued.
source: However, its mechanism has never been extensively pursued.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of the field, inferred from lack of literature on the topic.

claim: The various impacts of the salt taste sensation indicate multiple salt detection pathways in taste buds.
source: The various impacts of the salt taste sensation indicate multiple salt detection pathways in taste buds (Roper, 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Roper, 2015 and inference from the multifaceted nature of salt taste.

claim: The chloride ion participates in taste sensation because of the existence of the 'anion effect': the salty taste is most strongly perceived when the counter anion is a chloride ion.
source: Moreover, another component of table salt, the chloride ion, participates in taste sensation because of the existence of the 'anion effect': the salty taste is most strongly perceived when the counter anion is a chloride ion (Ye et al., 1991).
evidence: Supported by citation to Ye et al., 1991.

claim: Several reports suggested a certain cellular/molecular machinery underlying anion-sensitive Na+ detection or Cl− detection, which is independent of ENaC.
source: Several reports suggested a certain cellular/molecular machinery underlying anion-sensitive Na+ detection or Cl− detection, which is independent of ENaC (Lewandowski et al., 2016; Roebber et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to Lewandowski et al., 2016; Roebber et al., 2019.

claim: Transmembrane channel-like 4 (TMC4) expressed in taste buds involves high-concentration Cl− sensation.
source: Indeed, a recent study indicated that transmembrane channel-like 4 (TMC4) expressed in taste buds involves high-concentration Cl− sensation (Kasahara et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kasahara et al., 2021.

claim: No candidate molecule capable of sensing low or preferable concentrations of Cl− has been elucidated.
source: Nevertheless, no candidate molecule capable of sensing low or preferable concentrations of Cl− has been elucidated.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge in the field prior to the current study.

claim: The complete understanding of salt taste sensation, including the mechanism of chloride ion detection, remains unclear.
source: Therefore, the complete understanding of salt taste sensation, including the mechanism of chloride ion detection, remains unclear.
evidence: This is a summary statement about the state of knowledge, inferred from the gaps in understanding described.

claim: Sweet and umami sensations are understood through specific receptor proteins.
source: Unlike salt taste sensation, those for nutrients as sugars, amino acids, and nucleotides are understood as sweet and umami sensations through specific receptor proteins (Li et al., 2002; Nelson et al., 2002; Nelson et al., 2001).
evidence: Supported by citations to Li et al., 2002; Nelson et al., 2002; Nelson et al., 2001.

claim: Sweet and umami receptors are composed of taste receptor type 1 (T1r) proteins in the class C G-protein-coupled receptor (GPCR) family.
source: Sweet and umami receptors are composed of taste receptor type 1 (T1r) proteins in the class C G-protein-coupled receptor (GPCR) family.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field, supported by the cited literature.

claim: In humans, the T1r1/T1r3 heterodimer serves as the umami taste receptor and responds to amino acids as l-glutamate and aspartate, and nucleotides.
source: In humans, the T1r1/T1r3 heterodimer serves as the umami taste receptor and responds to amino acids as l-glutamate and aspartate, and nucleotides.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field.

claim: In humans, the T1r2/T1r3 heterodimer is the sweet taste receptor and responds to sugars.
source: In contrast, the T1r2/T1r3 heterodimer is the sweet taste receptor and responds to sugars.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field.

claim: The crystallographic structure of the medaka fish T1r2a/T1r3 extracellular ligand-binding domain (LBD) is currently the sole reported structure of T1rs.
source: We previously elucidated the crystallographic structure of the medaka fish T1r2a/T1r3 extracellular ligand-binding domain (LBD) (Nuemket et al., 2017), which is currently the sole reported structure of T1rs.
evidence: Supported by citation to Nuemket et al., 2017 and statement about the state of the field.

claim: In the medaka T1r2a/T1r3 structure, amino acid binding was observed in the middle of the LBD of T1r2a and T1r3 subunits.
source: In the structure, the amino acid binding was observed in the middle of the LBD of T1r2a and T1r3 subunits, which was consistent with the fact that T1r2a/T1r3 is an amino acid receptor (Oike et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to Nuemket et al., 2017 (previous work) and Oike et al., 2007.

claim: Medaka T1r2a/T1r3 is an amino acid receptor.
source: In the structure, the amino acid binding was observed in the middle of the LBD of T1r2a and T1r3 subunits, which was consistent with the fact that T1r2a/T1r3 is an amino acid receptor (Oike et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to Oike et al., 2007.

claim: Chloride ion binding was found in the vicinity of the amino acid-binding site in T1r3 in the medaka T1r2a/T1r3 structure.
source: Furthermore, chloride ion binding was found in the vicinity of the amino acid-binding site in T1r3 (Figure 2A).
evidence: Supported by crystallographic data from Nuemket et al., 2017 and Figure 2A showing the binding site.

claim: The physiological significance of Cl− binding for T1rs functions has remained unexplored.
source: So far, the physiological significance of Cl− binding for T1rs functions remains unexplored.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge prior to the current study.

claim: Chloride ions regulate other receptors in class C GPCRs, such as metabotropic glutamate receptors (mGluRs) and calcium-sensing receptors (CaSRs), and act as positive modulators for agonist binding.
source: Nevertheless, chloride ions regulate other receptors in class C GPCRs, such as metabotropic glutamate receptors (mGluRs) and calcium-sensing receptors (CaSRs), and act as positive modulators for agonist binding (Eriksen and Thomsen, 1995; Kuang and Hampson, 2006; Liu et al., 2020; Tora et al., 2018; Tora et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Eriksen and Thomsen, 1995; Kuang and Hampson, 2006; Liu et al., 2020; Tora et al., 2018; Tora et al., 2015.

claim: Cl− was coordinated at the binding site by the side-chain hydroxyl group of Thr105 and the main-chain amide groups of Gln148 and Ser149.
source: Cl− was coordinated at the binding site by the side-chain hydroxyl group of Thr105 and the main-chain amide groups of Gln148 and Ser149 (Figure 2D).
evidence: Supported by crystallographic structure data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The main-chain coordinating residues for Cl− (Gln148 and Ser149) are followed by Ser150, a critical residue for binding amino acid ligands.
source: These main-chain coordinating residues are followed by Ser150, a critical residue for binding amino acid ligands (Nuemket et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Nuemket et al., 2017.

claim: The loop regions where Thr105 and the Gln148–Ser150 locate are followed by helices B and C, respectively, which are essential structural units at the heterodimer interface.
source: Furthermore, the loop regions where Thr105 and the Gln148–Ser150 locate are followed by helices B and C, respectively. These helices are essential structural units at the heterodimer interface (Nuemket et al., 2017; Figure 2A).
evidence: Supported by citation to Nuemket et al., 2017 and Figure 2A showing the structural arrangement.

claim: Helices B and C are known to reorient upon agonist binding, resulting in conformation rearrangement of the subunits in the dimer, likely inducing receptor activation in class C GPCRs.
source: They are known to reorient upon agonist binding, resulting in conformation rearrangement of the subunits in the dimer, likely inducing receptor activation in class C GPCRs (Koehl et al., 2019; Kunishima et al., 2000).
evidence: Supported by citations to Koehl et al., 2019; Kunishima et al., 2000.

claim: The side-chain hydroxyl group of Ser149 serves as a cap for the positive helix dipole of helix C and simultaneously functions as a distal ligand for Cl− coordination.
source: In addition, the side-chain hydroxyl group of Ser149, which serves as a cap for the positive helix dipole of helix C, simultaneously functions as a distal ligand for Cl− coordination.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural data and knowledge of helix dipole interactions.

claim: The Cl− binding at this site is important for organizing the structure of the amino-acid-binding site and the heterodimer interface.
source: Therefore, the Cl− binding at this site is important for organizing the structure of the amino-acid-binding site and the heterodimer interface.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural location of the Cl− binding site and its proximity to key functional regions.

claim: Thr105, the residue that provides the side-chain-coordinating ligand for Cl− binding, is strictly conserved as either serine or threonine among T1r3s.
source: Thr105, the residue that provides the side-chain-coordinating ligand for Cl− binding, is strictly conserved as either serine or threonine among T1r3s.
evidence: Supported by sequence alignment data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: The amino acid sequence motifs surrounding the main-chain-coordinating ligands, FP45L and VIGPζ148ζ149, where 'ζ' is a hydrophilic amino acid, are well conserved to present the main-chain amide groups to coordinate Cl− with an appropriate geometry.
source: Additionally, the amino acid sequence motifs surrounding the main-chain-coordinating ligands, FP45L and VIGPζ148ζ149, where 'ζ' is a hydrophilic amino acid, are well conserved to present the main-chain amide groups to coordinate Cl− with an appropriate geometry.
evidence: Supported by sequence alignment data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: The Cl− binding site in T1r3 structurally corresponds to the Cl−-binding site in the hormone-binding domain of the atrial natriuretic peptide receptor (ANPR).
source: Notably, the site structurally corresponds to the Cl−-binding site in the hormone-binding domain of the atrial natriuretic peptide receptor (ANPR) (Figure 2F, G), in which Cl− positively regulates the peptide hormone binding (Misono, 2000).
evidence: Supported by structural comparison shown in Figure 2F, G and citation to Misono, 2000.

claim: In ANPR, Cl− positively regulates the peptide hormone binding.
source: Notably, the site structurally corresponds to the Cl−-binding site in the hormone-binding domain of the atrial natriuretic peptide receptor (ANPR) (Figure 2F, G), in which Cl− positively regulates the peptide hormone binding (Misono, 2000).
evidence: Supported by citation to Misono, 2000.

claim: The hormone-binding domain in ANPR shares a similar structural fold with LBD of T1rs and other class C GPCRs, and bacterial periplasmic-binding proteins.
source: Although ANPR is not a member of class C GPCR, the hormone-binding domain in ANPR shares a similar structural fold with LBD of T1rs and other class C GPCRs, and bacterial periplasmic-binding proteins (Kunishima et al., 2000; van den Akker et al., 2000).
evidence: Supported by citations to Kunishima et al., 2000; van den Akker et al., 2000.

claim: The conservation of the structure and the sequence motif at the Cl−-binding site at ANPR is also observed on mGluRs.
source: Accordingly, the conservation of the structure and the sequence motif at the Cl−-binding site at ANPR is also observed on mGluRs (Ogawa et al., 2010), and the importance of the site for receptor activation has been proposed (Acher et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to Ogawa et al., 2010 and Acher et al., 2011.

claim: The importance of the Cl− binding site for receptor activation has been proposed for mGluRs.
source: Accordingly, the conservation of the structure and the sequence motif at the Cl−-binding site at ANPR is also observed on mGluRs (Ogawa et al., 2010), and the importance of the site for receptor activation has been proposed (Acher et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Acher et al., 2011.

claim: Cl− binding at the site corresponding to that in T1r3 was observed in several mGluR and CaSR structures.
source: Indeed, Cl− binding at the site corresponding to that in T1r3 was observed in several mGluR and CaSR structures (Monn et al., 2015b; Zhang et al., 2016; Figure 2F, G) and was identified as a site regulating agonist binding (Liu et al., 2020; Tora et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Monn et al., 2015b; Zhang et al., 2016 and Figure 2F, G.

claim: The Cl− binding site in mGluR and CaSR was identified as a site regulating agonist binding.
source: Indeed, Cl− binding at the site corresponding to that in T1r3 was observed in several mGluR and CaSR structures (Monn et al., 2015b; Zhang et al., 2016; Figure 2F, G) and was identified as a site regulating agonist binding (Liu et al., 2020; Tora et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Liu et al., 2020; Tora et al., 2015.

claim: These results strongly imply the possibility that Cl− has some actions on T1r receptor functions.
source: These results strongly imply the possibility that Cl− has some actions on T1r receptor functions.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural conservation and functional roles in related receptors.

claim: Conservation at the Thr105 position was not observed among T1r1 and T1r2.
source: In contrast, conservation at the Thr105 position was not observed among T1r1 and T1r2 (Figure 2E).
evidence: Supported by sequence alignment data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: No significant anomalous peak derived from Br− or Cl− binding was observed in the crystal structure at the corresponding site in T1r2a.
source: Evidently, no significant anomalous peak derived from Br− or Cl− binding was observed in the crystal structure at the corresponding site in T1r2a (Figure 2B, C).
evidence: Supported by crystallographic data shown in Figure 2B, C.

claim: His100 in T1r2a, which corresponds to Thr105 in T1r3, adopted a significantly different side-chain conformation from that of Thr105 in T1r3.
source: His100 in T1r2a, which corresponds to Thr105 in T1r3, adopted a significantly different side-chain conformation from that of Thr105 in T1r3 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by structural data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: T1r1 and T1r2's ability to bind Cl− is unlikely.
source: Therefore, T1r1 and T1r2's ability to bind Cl− is unlikely.
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of conservation of key residues and absence of Cl− binding in structural data.

claim: The Br−-substituted crystal exhibited an anomalous peak at 8.5 σ in T1r2a, at a position close to the Lys265 side-chain ε-amino group.
source: In addition to the Cl−-binding site discussed above, the Br−-substituted crystal exhibited an anomalous peak at 8.5 σ in T1r2a, at a position close to the Lys265 side-chain ε-amino group (Figure 2B, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by crystallographic data shown in Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Cl− binding was not observed at the Lys265 site in the original Cl−-contained crystal.
source: Nevertheless, Cl− binding was not observed in the original Cl−-contained crystal.
evidence: Supported by the absence of anomalous peak at this position in the 2.7 Å data.

claim: The Lys265 site in T1r2a might have the ability to bind anions such as Br− or larger; but be not specific to Cl−.
source: Therefore, the site might have the ability to bind anions such as Br− or larger; but be not specific to Cl−.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation of Br− binding but not Cl− binding at this site.

claim: In human T1r1, the residue corresponding to Lys265 (Arg277) was suggested as a critical residue for activities of inosine monophosphate, an umami enhancer.
source: In human T1r1, the residue corresponding to Lys265 (Arg277) was suggested as a critical residue for activities of inosine monophosphate, an umami enhancer (Zhang et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to Zhang et al., 2008.

claim: The addition of Cl− to the Cl−-free T1r2a/T1r3LBD sample resulted in thermal stabilization of the protein.
source: The addition of Cl− to the Cl−-free T1r2a/T1r3LBD sample resulted in thermal stabilization of the protein (Figure 3A), which is indicative of Cl− binding to the protein.
evidence: Supported by DSF data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Thermal stabilization of T1r2a/T1r3LBD by Cl− is indicative of Cl− binding to the protein.
source: The addition of Cl− to the Cl−-free T1r2a/T1r3LBD sample resulted in thermal stabilization of the protein (Figure 3A), which is indicative of Cl− binding to the protein.
evidence: This is based on the principle that ligand binding typically stabilizes protein structure.

claim: The apparent Kd value for Cl− estimated by the melting temperatures (Tm) at various Cl− concentrations was ~110 µM.
source: The apparent Kd value for Cl− estimated by the melting temperatures (Tm) at various Cl− concentrations was ~110 µM (Figure 3B, Table 2).
evidence: Supported by DSF data shown in Figure 3B and Table 2.

claim: The Cl−-dependent thermal stabilization was confirmed by the fluorescence-detection size-exclusion chromatography-based thermostability (FSEC-TS) assay.
source: The Cl−-dependent thermal stabilization was confirmed by the fluorescence-detection size-exclusion chromatography-based thermostability (FSEC-TS) assay (Hattori et al., 2012; Figure 3C, Table 2).
evidence: Supported by FSEC-TS data shown in Figure 3C and Table 2, with citation to the method (Hattori et al., 2012).

claim: The Cl−-dependent stabilization was not observed on T1r2a/T1r3 with the Cl−-site mutation, T105A in T1r3.
source: However, the Cl−-dependent stabilization was not observed on T1r2a/T1r3 with the Cl−-site mutation, T105A in T1r3.
evidence: Supported by FSEC-TS data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: For the T105A mutant, the Tm values for both in the presence and absence of Cl− was similar to the values obtained for the wild-type (WT) protein in the absence of Cl−.
source: In the case of this mutant, the Tm values for both in the presence and absence of Cl− was similar to the values obtained for the wild-type (WT) protein in the absence of Cl− (Figure 3C, Figure 3—figure supplement 1, Table 2).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 3C, Figure 3—figure supplement 1, and Table 2.

claim: The Cl− effect on T1r2a/T1r3LBD is attributed to the identical site where the Cl− binding was observed in the crystal structure of T1r3.
source: These results indicate that the Cl− effect attributed to the identical site where the Cl− binding was observed in the crystal structure of T1r3.
evidence: This is inferred from the loss of Cl− effect in the T105A mutant.

claim: Class C GPCRs commonly exhibit agonist-induced conformational changes in LBD, such as the dimer rearrangement, which is essential for receptor activation and signaling.
source: Class C GPCRs commonly exhibit agonist-induced conformational changes in LBD, such as the dimer rearrangement, which is essential for receptor activation and signaling (Ellaithy et al., 2020; Koehl et al., 2019; Kunishima et al., 2000; Lin et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to Ellaithy et al., 2020; Koehl et al., 2019; Kunishima et al., 2000; Lin et al., 2021.

claim: T1r2a/T1r3LBD shows conformational change concomitant with the binding of amino acids, which can be detected as increased FRET intensity.
source: Consistent with this, we previously reported that T1r2a/T1r3LBD shows conformational change concomitant with the binding of amino acids, which can be detected as increased FRET intensity (Nango et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Nango et al., 2016.

claim: Adding Cl− to the fluorescent protein-fused T1r2a/T1r3LBD increased FRET intensities, similar to amino acids.
source: Notably, adding Cl− to the fluorescent protein-fused T1r2a/T1r3LBD also increased FRET intensities, similar to amino acids (Figure 3D).
evidence: Supported by FRET data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The EC50 for Cl−-induced FRET signal change was determined as ~1 mM.
source: The EC50 for Cl−-induced FRET signal change was determined as ~1 mM (Table 2).
evidence: Supported by FRET data shown in Table 2.

claim: The extent of the FRET change induced by Cl− was smaller than the changes induced by amino acids, such as ~1/2 of the latter.
source: Nevertheless, the extent of the FRET change induced by Cl− was smaller than the changes induced by amino acids, such as ~1/2 of the latter (Figure 3E).
evidence: Supported by FRET data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: The extent of the conformational change induced by Cl− is smaller than the change induced by amino acids.
source: Therefore, the results suggest that the extent of the conformational change induced by Cl− is smaller than the change induced by amino acids.
evidence: This is inferred from the smaller FRET change observed with Cl− compared to amino acids.

claim: The extent of Cl−-dependent FRET index change was reduced on T1r2a/T1r3 with the Cl−-site mutation, T105A in T1r3.
source: The extent of Cl−-dependent FRET index change was reduced on T1r2a/T1r3 with the Cl−-site mutation, T105A in T1r3 (Figure 3E).
evidence: Supported by FRET data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: The amino-acid-dependent FRET change in the T105A mutant was significantly reduced.
source: Considering that the amino-acid-dependent change in the mutant was also significantly reduced (Figure 3E), the T105A mutation on T1r3 might result in losing the ability of the conformational change induced by Cl− and amino acid bindings, although the possibility of deactivation of the protein during preparation due to its low stability cannot be excluded.
evidence: Supported by FRET data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: The T105A mutation on T1r3 might result in losing the ability of the conformational change induced by Cl− and amino acid bindings.
source: Considering that the amino-acid-dependent change in the mutant was also significantly reduced (Figure 3E), the T105A mutation on T1r3 might result in losing the ability of the conformational change induced by Cl− and amino acid bindings, although the possibility of deactivation of the protein during preparation due to its low stability cannot be excluded.
evidence: This is inferred from the reduced FRET changes for both Cl− and amino acids in the mutant.

claim: The Kd values for l-glutamine binding determined by ITC did not differ in the presence and absence of Cl−.
source: The Kd values for l-glutamine binding determined by ITC, as well as the EC50 values and the other parameters for l-glutamine-induced conformational change determined by FRET, did not differ in the presence and absence of Cl− (Figure 3F, Figure 3—figure supplement 1, and Table 2).
evidence: Supported by ITC data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1 and Table 2.

claim: The EC50 values and the other parameters for l-glutamine-induced conformational change determined by FRET did not differ in the presence and absence of Cl−.
source: The Kd values for l-glutamine binding determined by ITC, as well as the EC50 values and the other parameters for l-glutamine-induced conformational change determined by FRET, did not differ in the presence and absence of Cl− (Figure 3F, Figure 3—figure supplement 1, and Table 2).
evidence: Supported by FRET data shown in Figure 3F and Table 2.

claim: The Cl− binding had no significant effect on the binding of l-glutamine, a representative taste substance, at least for T1r2a/T1r3LBD from medaka fish.
source: These results indicated that the Cl− binding had no significant effect on the binding of l-glutamine, a representative taste substance, at least for T1r2a/T1r3LBD from medaka fish.
evidence: This is concluded from the ITC and FRET data showing no difference in l-glutamine binding parameters with or without Cl−.

claim: Biophysical studies on T1r2a/T1r3LBD from medaka fish suggested that Cl− binding to T1r3LBD induces a conformational change similar to that of an agonist without affecting agonist binding.
source: Biophysical studies on T1r2a/T1r3LBD from medaka fish suggested that Cl− binding to T1r3LBD induces a conformational change similar to that of an agonist without affecting agonist binding.
evidence: This is a summary of the biophysical results from DSF, FRET, and ITC experiments.

claim: Conventional cell-based receptor assay systems are affected by changes in extracellular ionic components.
source: While conventional cell-based receptor assay systems are affected by changes in extracellular ionic components, the application of various solutions to the taste pore side of the taste buds projected to taste nerve systems, are transduced exclusively as 'taste' signals, without inducing the other cellular responses derived from the ionic component changes in the surrounding environment.
evidence: This is based on general knowledge of cell-based assays and taste physiology.

claim: The application of various solutions to the taste pore side of the taste buds projected to taste nerve systems are transduced exclusively as 'taste' signals, without inducing the other cellular responses derived from the ionic component changes in the surrounding environment.
source: While conventional cell-based receptor assay systems are affected by changes in extracellular ionic components, the application of various solutions to the taste pore side of the taste buds projected to taste nerve systems, are transduced exclusively as 'taste' signals, without inducing the other cellular responses derived from the ionic component changes in the surrounding environment.
evidence: This is based on knowledge of taste bud physiology and the rationale for using nerve recordings.

claim: Nerve fibers that connect to T1r-expressing taste cells in WT mice receive taste information from cells likely possessing sweet (T1r2/T1r3) and umami (T1r1/T1r3) receptors.
source: We first identified nerve fibers that connect to T1r-expressing taste cells in WT mice, that is, that receive taste information from cells likely possessing sweet (T1r2/T1r3) and umami (T1r1/T1r3) receptors (Yasumatsu et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Yasumatsu et al., 2012 and the experimental approach.

claim: The identification of T1r-expressing nerve fibers was evidenced by responses to T1r agonists, such as sugars and amino acids, which were inhibited by gurmarin (Gur), a T1r-specific blocker.
source: The identification was evidenced by responses to T1r agonists, such as sugars and amino acids, which were inhibited by gurmarin (Gur), a T1r-specific blocker (Daly et al., 2013; Margolskee et al., 2007; Ninomiya and Imoto, 1995; Ninomiya et al., 1999).
evidence: Supported by citations to Daly et al., 2013; Margolskee et al., 2007; Ninomiya and Imoto, 1995; Ninomiya et al., 1999 and the experimental data.

claim: The fibers connecting to T1r-expressing cells exhibited responses induced by Cl−, which was applied as a form of NMDG-Cl devoid of the known salty taste stimulant, sodium ion.
source: Remarkably, the fibers also exhibited responses induced by Cl−, which was applied as a form of NMDG-Cl devoid of the known salty taste stimulant, sodium ion (Figure 4A).
evidence: Supported by nerve recording data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Cl−-induced impulse frequencies from the nerves increased in a concentration-dependent manner.
source: Cl−-induced impulse frequencies from the nerves increased in a concentration-dependent manner (Figure 4B).
evidence: Supported by nerve recording data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The responses to NMDG-Cl, NaCl, and KCl at the same concentrations did not differ significantly.
source: The responses to NMDG-Cl, NaCl, and KCl at the same concentrations did not differ significantly (repeated measures analysis of variance [ANOVA], p > 0.05), whereas responses to NMDG-gluconate were significantly smaller than those to NMDG-Cl (repeated measures ANOVA: F(1, 43) = 31.33, p < 0.001) and did not induce explicit responses up to 10 mM.
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of nerve recording data.

claim: Responses to NMDG-gluconate were significantly smaller than those to NMDG-Cl.
source: The responses to NMDG-Cl, NaCl, and KCl at the same concentrations did not differ significantly (repeated measures analysis of variance [ANOVA], p > 0.05), whereas responses to NMDG-gluconate were significantly smaller than those to NMDG-Cl (repeated measures ANOVA: F(1, 43) = 31.33, p < 0.001) and did not induce explicit responses up to 10 mM.
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of nerve recording data.

claim: NMDG-gluconate did not induce explicit responses up to 10 mM.
source: The responses to NMDG-Cl, NaCl, and KCl at the same concentrations did not differ significantly (repeated measures analysis of variance [ANOVA], p > 0.05), whereas responses to NMDG-gluconate were significantly smaller than those to NMDG-Cl (repeated measures ANOVA: F(1, 43) = 31.33, p < 0.001) and did not induce explicit responses up to 10 mM.
evidence: Supported by nerve recording data.

claim: The observed responses were attributed to Cl−.
source: These results confirmed that the observed responses were attributed to Cl−.
evidence: This is concluded from the comparison of responses to different chloride salts versus gluconate.

claim: All responses to Cl−, regardless of the type of counter cations, were significantly decreased by lingual treatment with Gur.
source: All responses to Cl−, regardless of the type of counter cations, were significantly decreased by lingual treatment with Gur (Figure 4B, repeated measures ANOVA: F(1, 42) = 56.65, p < 0.001 for NMDG-Cl; F(1, 50) = 24.78, p < 0.001 for NaCl; and F(1, 45) = 35.72, p < 0.001 for KCl).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of nerve recording data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Responses to Cl− in T1r3-KO mice were significantly lower than those in WT mice.
source: Furthermore, responses to Cl− in T1r3-KO mice were significantly lower than those in WT mice (repeated measures ANOVA: F(1, 43) = 25.36, p < 0.001; Figure 4C).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of nerve recording data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The observed Cl−-dependent responses were mediated by T1r.
source: The results indicate that the observed Cl−-dependent responses were mediated by T1r.
evidence: This is concluded from the gurmarin sensitivity and reduced responses in T1r3-KO mice.

claim: The Cl−-concentration range that induced nerve responses was lower (≤~10 mM) than that for Na+ detection by ENaC when applied as the NaCl form (≥~30 mM).
source: Notably, the Cl−-concentration range that induced nerve responses was lower (≤~10 mM) than that for Na+ detection by ENaC when applied as the NaCl form (≥~30 mM) (Chandrashekar et al., 2010) but is consistent with those for Cl−-binding and Cl−-induced conformational change observed on T1r2a/T1r3LBD (Table 2).
evidence: Supported by comparison of nerve recording data with literature on ENaC (Chandrashekar et al., 2010) and biophysical data in Table 2.

claim: The Cl−-concentration range that induced nerve responses is consistent with those for Cl−-binding and Cl−-induced conformational change observed on T1r2a/T1r3LBD.
source: Notably, the Cl−-concentration range that induced nerve responses was lower (≤~10 mM) than that for Na+ detection by ENaC when applied as the NaCl form (≥~30 mM) (Chandrashekar et al., 2010) but is consistent with those for Cl−-binding and Cl−-induced conformational change observed on T1r2a/T1r3LBD (Table 2).
evidence: Supported by comparison of nerve recording data with biophysical data in Table 2.

claim: A low Cl− concentration is sensorily detected via T1r in taste buds.
source: These results suggest that a low Cl− concentration is sensorily detected via T1r in taste buds.
evidence: This is concluded from the nerve recording data showing T1r-mediated responses to low Cl− concentrations.

claim: The responses induced by known taste substances for T1rs, such as sugars and amino acids, range from tens to hundreds of impulse frequencies per 10 s.
source: Although the responses induced by known taste substances for T1rs, such as sugars and amino acids, range from tens to hundreds of impulse frequencies per 10 s (Yasumatsu et al., 2012); the maximum response level induced by Cl− was low, ~10 per 10 s (Figure 4B).
evidence: Supported by citation to Yasumatsu et al., 2012.

claim: The maximum response level induced by Cl− was low, ~10 per 10 s.
source: Although the responses induced by known taste substances for T1rs, such as sugars and amino acids, range from tens to hundreds of impulse frequencies per 10 s (Yasumatsu et al., 2012); the maximum response level induced by Cl− was low, ~10 per 10 s (Figure 4B).
evidence: Supported by nerve recording data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Cl− likely produces a 'light' taste sensation compared with other known taste substances.
source: According to our observations, Cl− likely produces a 'light' taste sensation compared with other known taste substances.
evidence: This is inferred from the lower magnitude of nerve responses to Cl− compared to other T1r agonists.

claim: The response to l-glutamine or sucrose increased significantly by adding 10 mM NMDG-Cl.
source: As shown in Figure 4D, the response to l-glutamine or sucrose increased significantly by adding 10 mM NMDG-Cl (paired t-test, t2 = 7.56, p = 0.017 for l-glutamine and t2 = 5.05, p = 0.037 for sucrose).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of nerve recording data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: The responses to l-glutamine or sucrose with NMDG-Cl were suppressed by lingual treatment of Gur in the presence or absence of NMDG-Cl to a similar extent.
source: We confirmed that these responses had been suppressed by a lingual treatment of Gur in the presence (t2 = 6.73, p = 0.021 for l-glutamine and t2 = 8.80, p = 0.013 for sucrose) or absence (t2 = 8.32, p = 0.014 for l-glutamine and t2 = 11.72, p = 0.007 for sucrose) of NMDG-Cl to a similar extent and a similar level to the responses in T1r3-KO mice.
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of nerve recording data.

claim: The responses to the mixtures of Cl− with l-glutamine or sucrose did not differ significantly from the summation of the responses to each solution.
source: Moreover, the responses to the mixtures did not differ significantly from the summation of the responses to each solution (t2 = 2.34, p = 0.145 for l-glutamine and t2 = 2.31, p = 0.147 for sucrose).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of nerve recording data.

claim: The simultaneous binding of Cl− and a canonical taste substance, such as amino acids and sugars, to T1r do not cause synergistic responses.
source: The results suggest that the simultaneous binding of Cl− and a canonical taste substance, such as amino acids and sugars, to T1r do not cause synergistic responses.
evidence: This is concluded from the additive (not synergistic) nature of the responses to mixtures.

claim: Most reported behavioral assays for examining the gustatory detection of NaCl were performed with concentrations above ~30 mM, which can induce ENaC-mediated responses.
source: Thus far, most reported behavioral assays for examining the gustatory detection of NaCl were performed with concentrations above ~30 mM, which can induce ENaC-mediated responses.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of the literature on behavioral assays.

claim: A few reports have shown that NaCl solution induced higher consumption relative to water even below 10 mM concentration.
source: Nevertheless, a few reports have shown that NaCl solution induced higher consumption relative to water even below 10 mM concentration (Dyr et al., 2014; Stewart et al., 1994), which is below the range inducing ENaC-mediated responses (Chandrashekar et al., 2010) but within what we observed in the Cl−-induced taste nerve responses via T1r.
evidence: Supported by citations to Dyr et al., 2014; Stewart et al., 1994; Chandrashekar et al., 2010.

claim: NaCl consumption below 10 mM is below the range inducing ENaC-mediated responses but within the range of Cl−-induced taste nerve responses via T1r.
source: Nevertheless, a few reports have shown that NaCl solution induced higher consumption relative to water even below 10 mM concentration (Dyr et al., 2014; Stewart et al., 1994), which is below the range inducing ENaC-mediated responses (Chandrashekar et al., 2010) but within what we observed in the Cl−-induced taste nerve responses via T1r.
evidence: This is inferred from comparison of literature data with the current study's findings.

claim: The mouse preferred water containing 10 mM NMDG-Cl.
source: The mouse preferred water containing 10 mM NMDG-Cl, which was abolished by the application of Gur (Figure 4E, F).
evidence: Supported by two-bottle preference test data shown in Figure 4E, F.

claim: The preference for water containing 10 mM NMDG-Cl was abolished by the application of Gur.
source: The mouse preferred water containing 10 mM NMDG-Cl, which was abolished by the application of Gur (Figure 4E, F).
evidence: Supported by two-bottle preference test data shown in Figure 4E, F.

claim: Cl− is preferably perceived through taste signal transduction mediated by T1r.
source: These results suggest that Cl− is preferably perceived through taste signal transduction mediated by T1r.
evidence: This is concluded from the behavioral preference data and its sensitivity to gurmarin.

claim: Cl− is found to specifically interact with the LBD in T1r3, a common component of sweet and umami taste receptors, and induces a conformational change in the receptor's LBD region.
source: In this study, Cl− is found to specifically interact with the LBD in T1r3, a common component of sweet and umami taste receptors, and induces a conformational change in the receptor's LBD region.
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings from structural and biophysical studies.

claim: The Cl−-induced conformational change is similar to that induced by canonical taste substances for T1rs, amino acids, though its efficacy is slightly lower.
source: The Cl−-induced conformational change is similar to that induced by canonical taste substances for T1rs, amino acids, though its efficacy is slightly lower.
evidence: Supported by FRET data showing similar but smaller magnitude conformational changes.

claim: The structural change at LBD caused by Cl− binding most likely provokes receptor activation, resulting in G-protein activation in taste cells.
source: Therefore, as with other class C GPCRs, the structural change at LBD caused by Cl− binding most likely provokes receptor activation, resulting in G-protein activation in taste cells.
evidence: This is inferred from the conformational change data and knowledge of class C GPCR activation mechanisms.

claim: The signal from Cl− binding to T1r is considered to be transmitted through the common downstream cascade of T1rs: activation of phospholipase Cβ2 and resultant inositol triphosphate (IP3) production, IP3-dependent activation of IP3 receptors followed by Ca2+ release from endoplasmic reticulum, Ca2+-dependent activation of TRPM5 channel inducing taste cell depolarization, and subsequent action potential generation and neurotransmitter ATP release through CALHM1/3.
source: The signal is considered to be transmitted further through the common downstream cascade of T1rs: activation of phospholipase Cβ2 and resultant inositol triphosphate (IP3) production, IP3-dependent activation of IP3 receptors followed by Ca2+ release from endoplasmic reticulum, Ca2+-dependent activation of TRPM5 channel inducing taste cell depolarization, and subsequent action potential generation and neurotransmitter ATP release through CALHM1/3 (Taruno et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to Taruno et al., 2021 describing the T1r signaling cascade.

claim: The Cl− binding to T1r in taste cells is probably transmitted to the sweet taste nervous system, resulting in a light yet preferable taste sensation.
source: The Cl− binding to T1r in taste cells is thus probably transmitted to the sweet taste nervous system, resulting in a light yet preferable taste sensation.
evidence: This is inferred from the nerve recording and behavioral data showing T1r-mediated responses and preference.

claim: T1rs are conserved across vertebrates.
source: Since T1rs are conserved across vertebrates and the Cl−-binding site is likely conserved among T1r3 in various organisms, T1r-mediated Cl− responses might be common in many animals, such as humans.
evidence: This is based on general knowledge of T1r conservation.

claim: T1r-mediated Cl− responses might be common in many animals, such as humans.
source: Since T1rs are conserved across vertebrates and the Cl−-binding site is likely conserved among T1r3 in various organisms, T1r-mediated Cl− responses might be common in many animals, such as humans.
evidence: This is inferred from the conservation of T1rs and the Cl− binding site across species.

claim: The concentration range for the Cl−-induced conformational change of medaka T1r2a/T1r3LBD and increase in murine sweet nerve impulses (≤~10 mM) agrees with the NaCl concentration perceived as 'sweet' by humans.
source: Evidently, the concentration range for the Cl−-induced conformational change of medaka T1r2a/T1r3LBD and increase in murine sweet nerve impulses observed in this study (i.e., ≤~10 mM) agrees with the NaCl concentration perceived as 'sweet' by humans (Bartoshuk et al., 1964; Bartoshuk et al., 1978; Cardello, 1979; Figure 1).
evidence: Supported by comparison of current data with literature on human perception (Bartoshuk et al., 1964; Bartoshuk et al., 1978; Cardello, 1979) and Figure 1.

claim: The sweet sensation induced by NaCl was reportedly suppressed by topical application of Gymnema sylvestre, containing Gymnemic acids, which are specific inhibitors of human sweet taste receptor T1r2/T1r3.
source: Additionally, the sweet sensation induced by NaCl was reportedly suppressed by topical application of Gymnema sylvestre (Bartoshuk et al., 1978), containing Gymnemic acids, which are specific inhibitors of human sweet taste receptor T1r2/T1r3 (Sanematsu et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Bartoshuk et al., 1978 and Sanematsu et al., 2014.

claim: These findings agree with an earlier hypothesis by Bartoshuk et al. that dilute NaCl contains a sweet stimulus that interacts with the same receptor molecules as sucrose.
source: These findings agree with an earlier hypothesis by Bartoshuk et al. that dilute NaCl contains a sweet stimulus that interacts with the same receptor molecules as sucrose (Bartoshuk et al., 1978).
evidence: Supported by citation to Bartoshuk et al., 1978 and comparison with current findings.

claim: The reported 'sweet' sensation by low NaCl concentration faded out at the concentrations detected as 'salty'.
source: The reported 'sweet' sensation by low NaCl concentration faded out at the concentrations detected as 'salty' (Bartoshuk et al., 1964; Bartoshuk et al., 1978; Cardello, 1979), thereby agreeing with the fact that we might be unaware that table salt is sweet at such concentrations.
evidence: Supported by citations to Bartoshuk et al., 1964; Bartoshuk et al., 1978; Cardello, 1979.

claim: The phenomenon of sweet sensation fading at higher salt concentrations could be explained by 'mixture suppression', such that a light sweet sensation is masked by an intense salty sensation in a higher concentration range of NaCl.
source: The phenomenon could be explained by 'mixture suppression' (Bartoshuk, 1975; Keast and Breslin, 2003; Stevens, 1996), such that a light sweet sensation is masked by an intense salty sensation in a higher concentration range of NaCl.
evidence: Supported by citations to Bartoshuk, 1975; Keast and Breslin, 2003; Stevens, 1996 and inference about sensory interactions.

claim: The Cl− perception at low salt concentrations is achieved via the T1rs-mediating taste system, which transduces information as a preferred taste by nature.
source: The Cl− perception at low salt concentrations found in this study is achieved via the T1rs-mediating taste system, which transduces information as a preferred taste by nature.
evidence: This is concluded from the nerve recording and behavioral data showing T1r-mediated responses and preference.

claim: This system might serve as another pathway for preferred salt perception promoting intake along with the pathway for Na+ perception as a preferred taste via taste cells that express the Na+ receptor ENaC and a purinergic neurotransmission channel CALHM1/3.
source: Since Cl− is also a component of table salt, this system might serve as another pathway for preferred salt perception promoting intake along with the pathway for Na+ perception as a preferred taste via taste cells that express the Na+ receptor ENaC and a purinergic neurotransmission channel CALHM1/3 (Nomura et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Nomura et al., 2020 and inference about multiple salt detection pathways.

claim: The T1r-mediated Cl− sensing shows different properties from those of cells or molecules reportedly exhibiting anion-sensitive Na+ detection or Cl− detection in taste buds thus far.
source: In contrast, the T1r-mediated Cl− sensing observed in this study shows several different properties from those of cells or the molecules reportedly exhibiting anion-sensitive Na+ detection or Cl− detection in taste buds thus far.
evidence: This is concluded from comparison with literature on other Cl− detection pathways.

claim: The anion-sensitive Na+-responding taste cells reported by Lewandowski et al. are type 3 cells, which include sour- but not sweet-responding cells.
source: Specifically, the anion-sensitive Na+-responding taste cells reported by Lewandowski et al. are type 3 cells, which include sour- but not sweet-responding cells (Lewandowski et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Lewandowski et al., 2016.

claim: The Cl−-detection pathway reported by Roebber et al. was observed in type 2 cells, which include both sweet- and bitter-responding cells, but was inhibited by a blocker of phospholipase C, which mediates sweet- and bitter-signaling downstream of T1r and bitter receptors.
source: The Cl−-detection pathway reported by Roebber et al. was observed in type 2 cells, which include both sweet- and bitter-responding cells, but was inhibited by a blocker of phospholipase C, which mediates sweet- and bitter-signaling downstream of T1r and bitter receptors (Roebber et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Roebber et al., 2019.

claim: The Cl− responses mediated by TMC4 were observed in the glossopharyngeal nerve but not in the CT nerve wherein T1r-mediated responses were observed.
source: The Cl− responses mediated by TMC4 were observed in the glossopharyngeal nerve but not in the CT nerve wherein T1r-mediated responses were observed (Kasahara et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kasahara et al., 2021.

claim: Responses by the reported high Cl−-responsive pathways were tested by much higher concentrations of NaCl, typically in the several hundred mM range, than those used in this study.
source: Notably, responses by these reported pathways were tested by much higher concentrations of NaCl, typically in the several hundred mM range (Kasahara et al., 2021; Lewandowski et al., 2016; Roebber et al., 2019), than those used in this study.
evidence: Supported by citations to Kasahara et al., 2021; Lewandowski et al., 2016; Roebber et al., 2019.

claim: There may be multiple distinct concentration-dependent pathways for Cl− detection in taste buds.
source: These results imply that there may be multiple distinct concentration-dependent pathways for Cl− detection in taste buds.
evidence: This is inferred from the differences between the current findings and previous reports on Cl− detection.

claim: High NaCl concentration is transduced as an aversive taste through bitter and sour taste cells.
source: Given that high NaCl concentration is transduced as an aversive taste through bitter and sour taste cells (Oka et al., 2013), the relevance between the reported high Cl−-responsive pathways and high NaCl responses by bitter and sour cells is of interest, as pointed out by the previous studies, and will require further investigation.
evidence: Supported by citation to Oka et al., 2013.

claim: The relevance between the reported high Cl−-responsive pathways and high NaCl responses by bitter and sour cells is of interest and will require further investigation.
source: Given that high NaCl concentration is transduced as an aversive taste through bitter and sour taste cells (Oka et al., 2013), the relevance between the reported high Cl−-responsive pathways and high NaCl responses by bitter and sour cells is of interest, as pointed out by the previous studies, and will require further investigation.
evidence: This is a statement about future research directions.

claim: Salt taste sensation and natriuresis are critical physiological processes that regulate sodium intake and excretion to maintain body fluid homeostasis.
source: Salt taste sensation and natriuresis are critical physiological processes that regulate sodium intake and excretion to maintain body fluid homeostasis.
evidence: This is based on general physiological knowledge.

claim: Both salt taste sensation and natriuresis use the counter anion Cl− to regulate the molecular functions of the receptors, T1rs and ANPRs, which share a similar extracellular protein architecture with a conserved Cl−-binding site.
source: Intriguingly, both processes were found to use the counter anion Cl− to regulate the molecular functions of the receptors, T1rs and ANPRs, which share a similar extracellular protein architecture with a conserved Cl−-binding site.
evidence: This is concluded from the structural and functional similarities between T1rs and ANPRs regarding Cl− binding.

claim: In the case of ANPR, mGluRs, and CaSR, positive allosteric modulations by Cl− for agonist binding have been observed, with some variations in the extent of the enhancement.
source: In the case of ANPR, mGluRs, and CaSR, positive allosteric modulations by Cl− for agonist binding have been observed, with some variations in the extent of the enhancement (Eriksen and Thomsen, 1995; Kuang and Hampson, 2006; Liu et al., 2020; Tora et al., 2018; Tora et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Eriksen and Thomsen, 1995; Kuang and Hampson, 2006; Liu et al., 2020; Tora et al., 2018; Tora et al., 2015.

claim: Whether the Cl− actions on T1rs of other subtypes or from other organisms have some variance is yet to be examined.
source: Whether the Cl− actions on T1rs of other subtypes or from other organisms have some variance is yet to be examined.
evidence: This is a statement about future research needs.
